title: Following
coreIdea: Stay with one moving subject for a short period and photograph the evolving relationship between the person and their environment.
whyItMatters: It teaches sustained observation and the ability to build a small narrative through changing positions rather than isolated hits. It also forces you to manage distance, presence, and ethics in real time — skills that directly improve both candid street work and approached street portraits.
shootingBrief: Choose one subject moving through public space. Follow discreetly for 5–12 minutes. Make a series showing different interactions with the surroundings. Stop immediately if the person notices and shows discomfort. Minimum coherent set of 6–8 frames. Volume 40–60.
technicalFocus: Settings: AF-C, f/4–5.6, shutter 1/250s or faster.
Focusing: Continuous on the subject.
Stance: Parallel or slightly behind, never aggressive or predatory. Keep your body language neutral.
Light: Work with what the path offers.
Distance: Maintain respectful working distance (usually 4–10 meters). The longer end of the 24-50mm helps.
Primarily candid. If engagement happens, it ends the exercise for that subject.
failureModes: Getting too close too fast.
Producing only similar frames from the same angle.
Ignoring clear discomfort signals.
Turning the follow into a chase.

goodVsExcellent.good: A series of the same person in different places.
goodVsExcellent.excellent: The series shows genuine change in the relationship between person and place, and the strongest single frame could stand alone with clear narrative weight.

reflectionPrompts: What worked and what failed against the constraint?
Strongest frame and why it succeeds.
What will you carry into the next session?
sources: Maciej Dakowicz on presence and not being afraid.
Winogrand footage for energy of moving with the street.
Practical discussions of distance and ethics in following.
Winogrand’s sustained public energy. Phil Penman’s denser New York following work. Clear ethical boundaries from long-working street photographers.

title: Behind
coreIdea: Photograph people primarily from behind or strong three-quarter rear so posture, clothing, gesture, and context carry the picture.
whyItMatters: It removes reliance on facial expression — the crutch of weak street photography. You are forced to read body language, clothing as character, and the relationship between figure and environment. These skills improve every picture that includes people, including approached street portraits.
shootingBrief: Only rear or strong three-quarter rear angles. Minimum 8 frames where the absence of a full face is a strength, not a weakness. Volume 40–70. Dignity is non-negotiable.
technicalFocus: Settings: f/4–5.6, shutter fast enough for gesture.
Focusing: On the upper body or the strongest graphic element of the figure.
Stance: Slightly lower or matching the subject’s direction of movement.
Light: Backlight and side light are powerful for separation and silhouette.
Distance: 2–6 meters.
Candid. Never make the person look mocked, diminished, or vulnerable.
failureModes: Weak or neutral posture.
Cluttered backgrounds that compete with the figure.
Making the person look small or exploited.
Including just enough face that the constraint is broken without gaining expression.

goodVsExcellent.good: No full face and the picture is still readable.
goodVsExcellent.excellent: Posture, clothing, and environment create a complete character or story. The absence of the face feels like a deliberate strength.

reflectionPrompts: What worked and what failed against the constraint?
Strongest frame and why it succeeds.
What will you carry into the next session?
sources: Vivian Maier composition analyses (many of her strongest frames work without full face).
Elliott Erwitt timing and gesture.
Practical body-language reading in street work.
Vivian Maier’s rear and three-quarter work. Erwitt’s gesture-driven pictures. Gustavo Minas’ quieter rear figures.

title: Looking Down
coreIdea: Change viewpoint completely. Work the ground plane — feet, shadows, discarded objects, patterns, reflections in pavement.
whyItMatters: Default eye-level is a habit, not a law. Many strong pictures exist only at different heights. Looking down forces new subject matter and breaks compositional autopilot. It also trains edge control and the ability to make complete frames from limited information.
shootingBrief: Entire session looking downward. Subjects: feet and shoes, shadows, sidewalk textures, accidental compositions of litter, puddle reflections, etc. Minimum 8 intentional frames. Volume 40–60. Include both tight details and wider overhead views when possible (stairs, bridges, upper windows).
technicalFocus: Settings: Higher shutter (1/320s+) to freeze hand movement while looking down.
Focusing: Single-point or zone on the ground plane.
Stance: Control your own shadow rigorously. It is the most common failure.
Light: Hard light creates the best ground graphics and shadows.
Distance: From waist height to true overhead.
Candid or pure still life of the street surface.
failureModes: Including your own feet or shadow by accident.
Pure texture with no point or hierarchy.
Weak edges and messy corners.
Making the frame feel accidental rather than chosen.

goodVsExcellent.good: Something interesting on the ground is recorded.
goodVsExcellent.excellent: The downward view creates a complete, self-contained world that feels intentional. The frame has clear structure and would not work at eye level.

reflectionPrompts: What worked and what failed against the constraint?
Strongest frame and why it succeeds.
What will you carry into the next session?
sources: Vivian Maier analyses covering lower angles and ground work.
Joel Meyerowitz on changing viewpoint and quality of observation.
Practical overhead and ground-level street examples.
Vivian Maier’s lower and ground-level frames. Erwitt’s occasional downward humor. Saul Leiter’s more abstract ground and reflection work.

title: Blurred
coreIdea: Use intentional motion blur (panning or static camera with moving subjects) as the primary quality of the picture.
whyItMatters: Sharpness is a default, not a requirement. Controlled blur can carry energy, atmosphere, and time in ways that sharp frames cannot. Learning when and how to use it expands your visual vocabulary and prevents you from rejecting pictures simply because they are not tack-sharp.
shootingBrief: Shutter speeds roughly 1/15s to 1/4s (experiment). Two methods: (a) panning with a moving subject, (b) static camera with moving people or traffic creating streaks. Minimum 6 frames where blur is clearly intentional and successful. Volume 40–70. Cull pure failures on the camera.
technicalFocus: Settings: Shutter priority or full manual. Start around 1/15s and adjust. Raise ISO if needed to keep aperture in a usable range (f/4–8).
Focusing: Pre-focus on the subject plane or use continuous.
Stance: Brace against a post, railing, or wall for static-camera blur. For panning, smooth horizontal movement from the hips, not the arms.
Light: Overcast or lower light helps keep shutter slow without extreme filters.
Distance: Medium for panning; any for static streaks.
Candid.
failureModes: Blur that looks like a mistake rather than a decision.
No clear subject still readable inside the blur.
Camera shake that is uncontrolled rather than directional.
Accepting frames where everything is equally soft.

goodVsExcellent.excellent: The blur has clear direction and energy, and a subject still reads inside it. The picture feels more alive than a sharp version of the same scene would.

reflectionPrompts: What worked and what failed against the constraint?
Strongest frame and why it succeeds.
What will you carry into the next session?
sources: Practical panning and slow-shutter street demonstrations.
Trent Parke related material for radical use of light and motion (when available).
Technical breakdowns of intentional blur in street contexts.
Trent Parke’s more extreme motion and light work. Certain Winogrand frames that accept blur as part of the energy of the street.

title: Layers
coreIdea: Build frames with clear foreground, midground, and background that interact without collapsing into clutter.
whyItMatters: Depth and controlled complexity separate competent street pictures from flat ones. Layers create visual richness and allow multiple points of interest to coexist. This is a core skill in the work of Alex Webb, Joel Meyerowitz, and the denser frames of Winogrand. It also improves street portraits by teaching you to place a person inside a meaningful environment rather than against a clean backdrop.
shootingBrief: Actively seek three-plane compositions. Look for overlapping people, architecture, reflections, or foliage that create depth. Minimum 6 frames with clear, readable layers. Volume 40–70. Test both the wider and longer ends of the 24-50mm.
technicalFocus: Settings: f/8–11 preferred for multi-plane sharpness on APS-C.
Focusing: Usually on the midground or the strongest subject plane.
Stance: Move your feet to control overlaps and avoid merges (elements that touch and flatten the space).
Light: Side light or backlight helps separate planes. Flat light kills layer separation.
Distance: Wider end exaggerates depth; longer end compresses layers. Both are valid — choose deliberately.
Candid. People are often the connecting tissue between planes.
failureModes: Uncontrolled merges that flatten the image.
Too many planes with no hierarchy.
Flat light that removes separation.
Focusing on the wrong plane so the key relationship is soft.

goodVsExcellent.excellent: The planes interact (through gesture, gaze, graphic echo, or light) and the picture remains clear and organized rather than busy.

reflectionPrompts: What worked and what failed against the constraint?
Strongest frame and why it succeeds.
What will you carry into the next session?
sources: Joel Meyerowitz on complex street frames and observation.
Analyses of layered street work (Alex Webb style references are useful here).
Nick Turpin on constructing frames with multiple elements.
Alex Webb’s dense color layers (strong reference for this exercise). Cartier-Bresson’s cleaner geometric layers. Gustavo Minas’ precise, quieter layering. Meyerowitz’s more complex color street.
